criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural communal drinking-water supply (handpump boreholes and community waterpoints) and household/community water access, management, and use in Ethiopia, Malawi, and Uganda.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study centrally investigates community-based water governance institutions (Waterpoint Committees, iddirs, village chiefs, LC1 chairpersons, kebele officials) and national decentralisation/WASH policy frameworks. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although the overarching framing ('working with the grain' / institutional bricolage) and Figure 2 emphasize the organizational form of water management arrangements, the empirical analysis directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access: local service-provider governance/ownership structure (state-mandated committees vs chiefs, iddirs, and private caretakers with boreholes on their compounds), tariff and cost-recovery rules (stringent user fees, seasonal payment rules), discretion and accommodation (free water exemptions for the poorest vs priority for higher-paying commercial resellers), enforcement sanctions (fines and physically locking boreholes to enforce rules or meeting attendance), and religious exclusion rules.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical evidence from a multi-country study: a 2-day qualitative social survey of 150 community waterpoints across 12 districts in Ethiopia, Malawi, and Uganda (300 fieldwork days, ~500 documents), a yearlong longitudinal study of 12 communities in Malawi and Uganda with 30 participant diary keepers, national political economy analyses (16-21 stakeholder interviews per country), and district sustainability assessments. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: While quantitative waterpoint functionality data from Phase 1 are published elsewhere and Figure 2 reports the organizational composition of water management arrangements, Phases 2 and 3 empirically report qualitative outcomes directly relevant to household/community access, affordability, service continuity, and exclusion: pricing out of poorer community members under stringent user-fee regimes, preferential access for commercial water sellers, free-water accommodations for the poorest households, coercive denial/restriction of access via borehole locking, exclusion of people of particular faiths, and reciprocal inter-village waterpoint access during breakdowns.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (rural communities, communal waterpoints/WMAs, and community water users across Ethiopia, Malawi, and Uganda), governance/rule-type exposures, qualitative access/exclusion outcomes, and multi-phase qualitative study design are clearly identified.

evidence_quotes.quote: We examine water management arrangements by undertaking an in-depth social survey of 150 communities in the three countries. We also undertake yearlong studies in 12 communities in Malawi and Uganda involving 30 diary keepers.
we tracked community members’ day-to-day experiences of managing, accessing, and using water.

For example, in one longitudinal case study the ﬁnancial incentive of a powerful individual to maintain the waterpoint in good working order coupled with a stringent user fee system that the poorer members of the community could not afford. In other cases, users who pay a higher fee, for example those who then proﬁt from selling the water they draw, are favoured over regular water users.
Beyond locking the borehole so that it is only used during the daytime, the chairperson locks it to enforce decisions or to make people attend meetings.
He instructs the chairperson not to overcharge people and to let the poorest community members take water for free.
Among these principles, we observe patriarchal tendencies that relegate the decision-making power of women vis-à-vis men, or the exclusion of people of particular faiths.

raw_response.exposure: Community-based water governance and rule-type access mechanisms: state-mandated Waterpoint Committees (WPCs) versus hybrid/informal local management structures (Ethiopian iddirs and kebele officials, Malawian village chiefs, Ugandan LC1 chairpersons, and personalised borehole caretakers), including user-fee/cost-recovery rules, seasonal payment schedules, discretionary fee exemptions for the poor, coercive rule enforcement (fines and physical borehole locking), and exclusionary social/religious norms
raw_response.outcome: Qualitative community and household rural water access, affordability, continuity, and exclusion outcomes (affordability exclusion of poorer households under stringent user fees, preferential access for higher-paying commercial water vendors, fee exemptions enabling free access for the poorest, coercive restriction of access via borehole locking, faith-based exclusion, and reciprocal inter-village waterpoint access during breakdowns), alongside the organizational form and capacity of water management arrangements
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural communities and communal groundwater waterpoints (handpump boreholes/wells) and their water management arrangements: 150 community waterpoints across 12 districts (4 per country in Ethiopia, Malawi, and Uganda) in Phase 2, plus 12 rural communities in 4 districts of Malawi and Uganda with 30 community diary keepers over one year in Phase 3, alongside 16-21 sector interviews per country for national political economy analyses and district sustainability workshops
raw_response.rationale: Include (medium confidence). This multi-country qualitative socio-legal/institutional study of rural communal water supply in Ethiopia, Malawi, and Uganda (150 surveyed communities plus 12 yearlong diary-study communities) satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Although its overarching theoretical focus is on 'working with the grain' and the organizational composition of community water management arrangements (leaving quantitative Phase 1 functionality data to a companion paper), its empirical findings directly document rule-type governance mechanisms governing service access—local service-provider ownership/management structure (formal WPCs vs chiefs, iddirs, and private caretakers), user-fee/cost-recovery rules, seasonal fee enforcement, discretionary fee exemptions for the poorest, coercive borehole locking, and religious exclusion—and report qualitative outcomes on household affordability, access restrictions, exclusion, and reciprocal backup access during breakdowns. Per protocol, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies with clear mechanism and access/exclusion evidence are included for the mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Multi-country qualitative extensive-intensive empirical study (in-depth qualitative social survey of 150 communities, yearlong longitudinal diary and fieldwork study in 12 communities, country-level political economy analyses, and district sustainability assessments)
